## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** State of the art (as of July 2026) in AI coding-agent governance and harness design — the problem space of the claude.md-workflow repo: project instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md-style), lifecycle hooks, deterministic verification gates, persistent agent memory/working-state across sessions and compaction, behavioral guardrails against scope creep/overclaiming/sycophancy, git-level enforcement, task contracts, and parallel multi-agent orchestration (worktree isolation, orchestrator/reduce patterns, adversarial review). Survey and compare best practices from: Anthropic (Claude Code, Agent SDK, skills/hooks/subagents), OpenAI (Codex, AGENTS.md), Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), Microsoft (GitHub Copilot agents, AutoGen/agent frameworks), NVIDIA (agent toolkits/NeMo), xAI (Grok agents/coding); and non-Western labs: Moonshot AI (Kimi K2.5 agentic training), Zhipu/Z.ai (GLM-5.x coding agents), DeepSeek (agentic/tool-use practices), Tencent (recent Hunyuan model launch and agent tooling), MiniMax (M-series agentic models), Alibaba Qwen if relevant; plus respected independents: Nous Research (Hermes 4/Hermes agent), Fundamental Research Labs (Peter Wang co-founder), the team behind the Ornith-1.0 LLM, tinygrad/George Hotz's approach to minimal harnesses, and any other influential open agent-harness projects (e.g. OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin/Cognition). For each: what they prescribe for instruction-file structure and length, memory persistence, verification/eval gating, multi-agent patterns, and prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement. Identify convergent consensus, notable divergences (especially Western vs Chinese lab practices), and concrete, citable insights that should shape a 2026 rewrite of a drop-in governance kit for coding agents. Note if any named entity cannot be verified to exist (e.g. 'Ornith-1.0') rather than guessing.

24 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] Anthropic officially prescribes keeping CLAUDE.md short and aggressively pruned, warning that over-long instruction files cause the model to ignore instructions — the recommended test for each line is whether removing it would cause mistakes.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (primary)
Quote: "Keep it concise. For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!"
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices live on 2026-07-14 (official Anthropic Claude Code docs). The exact quoted sentence appears verbatim in the "Write an effective CLAUDE.md" section: "Keep it concise. For each line, ask: 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!" The claim's three elements are all directly supported: (1) prescribe short/pruned files — the page also says "keep it short and human-readable", "prune it regularly", and lists "The over-specified CLAUDE.md" as a named failure pattern with the fix "Ruthlessly prune"; (2) warning that over-long files cause ignored instructions — "If your CLAUDE.md is too long, Claude ignores half of it because important rules get lost in the noise" and "If Claude keeps doing something you don't want despite having a rule against it, the file is probably too long and the rule is getting lost"; (3) the removal test is quoted verbatim. Source is the primary, current, official vendor documentation — exactly matching the claim's framing as what "Anthropic officially prescribes." No overreach detected: the claim does not exaggerate beyond the doc's wording. Not outdated (page is the live current best-practices doc referencing 2026-era features like auto mode and agent teams), and not marketing — it is prescriptive usage guidance including admissions of model failure modes.

### [1] Anthropic draws an explicit prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement line: CLAUDE.md instructions are advisory while hooks are deterministic, and hooks should be used for actions that must happen every time; a Stop hook can block turn completion until a check passes, with an override after 8 consecutive blocks.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (primary)
Quote: "Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices live (2026-07-14). All three components of the claim appear verbatim: (1) "Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens" (Set up hooks section); (2) "Use hooks for actions that must happen every time with zero exceptions"; (3) "As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks" (Give Claude a way to verify its work section). The hooks reference page (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) corroborates that Stop hooks block via exit code 2 / decision:"block" ("Prevents Claude from stopping, continues the conversation") and contains nothing contradicting the 8-block override, which is documented on the best-practices page. Source is Anthropic's official primary documentation about its own product — authoritative for a claim about what Anthropic prescribes, and current.

### [2] Anthropic's top verification prescription is to give the agent a runnable pass/fail check (tests, build exit code, linter, screenshot diff) and offers an escalation ladder of gating strictness: in-prompt iteration, /goal conditions re-checked every turn, deterministic Stop hooks, and second-opinion verification subagents.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (primary)
Quote: "As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks."
Verifier evidence (high): Live fetch of https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (2026-07-14) confirms every element. The section "Give Claude a way to verify its work" is the first best-practice section on the page and lists exactly the claimed check types: "a test suite, a build exit code, a linter, a script that diffs output against a fixture, or a browser screenshot compared against a design." The four-rung escalation ladder appears verbatim under "Once the check exists, decide how hard it gates the stop": (1) "In one prompt: ask Claude to run the check and iterate in the same message"; (2) "Across a session: set the check as a /goal condition. A separate evaluator re-checks it after every turn and Claude keeps working until it holds"; (3) "As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes. Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks" (the supporting quote, verified verbatim); (4) "By a second opinion: a verification subagent or a dynamic workflow that checks its own findings has a fresh model try to refute the result." The "top prescription" characterization is defensible: it is the lead best practice and is reinforced later ("Always provide verification... If you can't verify it, don't ship it"). Primary official source, current, non-marketing prescriptive docs — source quality matches claim strength.

### [3] For multi-agent orchestration, Anthropic recommends git-worktree-isolated parallel sessions, agent teams with a team lead, Writer/Reviewer session pairs, and adversarial review by a fresh-context subagent that sees only the diff and criteria — while warning that reviewers prompted to find gaps will over-report, causing over-engineering.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices (primary)
Quote: "A reviewer running in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change, so it evaluates the result on its own terms."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched the primary source (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) on 2026-07-14 and confirmed every element verbatim: (1) "Worktrees: run separate CLI sessions in isolated git checkouts so edits don't collide"; (2) "Agent teams: automated coordination of multiple sessions with shared tasks, messaging, and a team lead"; (3) an explicit "Writer/Reviewer pattern" table with Session A (Writer) / Session B (Reviewer); (4) the "Add an adversarial review step" section contains the exact supporting quote about a fresh subagent seeing only the diff and criteria; (5) the over-reporting warning appears verbatim in a callout: "A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering: extra abstraction layers, defensive code, and tests for cases that can't happen." The claim is a faithful summary of a current, primary, first-party source stating what Anthropic recommends — exactly the right source type for this claim. Minor nuance only: worktrees are listed as one of four parallel-session options (worktrees, desktop app, web, agent teams), which the claim does not misrepresent.

### [4] OpenAI Codex automatically loads project instruction files before starting any task: it reads AGENTS.md files as a mandatory pre-work step, making the instruction file the primary governance mechanism rather than an optional hint.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md (primary)
Quote: "Codex reads `AGENTS.md` files before doing any work."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified against the primary source. https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md (308-redirects to https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md, OpenAI's current Codex docs) contains the quoted sentence verbatim: "Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work," and specifies this happens automatically once per run/session at startup, with a hierarchical discovery chain (global ~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md and AGENTS.md, then project files from Git root to cwd, nearer files overriding). So the core factual assertion — automatic, harness-level loading of AGENTS.md as a pre-work step, not an opt-in feature — is directly supported by current first-party documentation, and AGENTS.md is OpenAI's designated instruction/configuration mechanism for Codex. One qualification the claim should carry but which does not refute it: loading is mandatory, compliance is not. The docs make no guarantee instructions are followed, there is a 32 KiB default truncation limit (project_doc_max_bytes), and multiple open openai/codex GitHub issues (#6502, #6666, #4466, #3420, #25884) document Codex reading AGENTS.md yet inconsistently applying it. The claim as worded ("reads... as a mandatory pre-work step") stays on the supported side — it asserts mandatory reading, not enforced obedience — so "primary governance mechanism" is accurate in the prompt-injection sense, though any downstream write-up should note enforcement remains prompt-level and advisory, not deterministic.

### [5] Codex resolves instruction files via a three-tier hierarchy — global (~/.codex, checking AGENTS.override.md then AGENTS.md), then project scope walking from the Git root down to the current directory — with at most one file loaded per directory and nested files taking precedence over ancestors.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md (primary)
Quote: "Files closer to your current directory override earlier guidance"
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched the cited primary source (https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md, 308-redirects to https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md). It confirms all four components verbatim: (1) global scope — "In your Codex home directory (defaults to ~/.codex...), Codex reads AGENTS.override.md if it exists. Otherwise, Codex reads AGENTS.md"; (2) project walk — "Starting at the project root (typically the Git root), Codex walks down to your current working directory... it checks for AGENTS.override.md, then AGENTS.md"; (3) "Codex includes at most one file per directory."; (4) "Files closer to your current directory override earlier guidance because they appear later." Current official OpenAI vendor documentation, not marketing; the supporting quote is accurate and the claim does not overreach it. Minor cosmetic quibble only: "three-tier" framing (global + root-to-cwd walk) is a paraphrase, not a mechanical error.

### [6] OpenAI imposes a hard deterministic size cap on combined instruction-file content: the default project_doc_max_bytes limit is 32 KiB, and Codex silently stops including additional AGENTS.md files once that budget is exhausted — the docs recommend splitting instructions across nested directories rather than one large file.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md (primary)
Quote: "Codex stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit"
Verifier evidence (high): Primary source verified live (2026-07-14): the OpenAI Codex docs (developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md, redirecting to learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md) state verbatim "Codex skips empty files and stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit defined by project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB by default)" and "Raise the limit or split instructions across nested directories when you hit the cap." The "silently" qualifier is corroborated by openai/codex GitHub issue #7138 ("AGENTS.md is silently truncated without any warning within the TUI"). Only nuance: docs offer raising the limit (config.toml project_doc_max_bytes) as an alternative to splitting, so the cap is a configurable default rather than absolute — a simplification, not an error; the claim correctly says "default".

### [7] AGENTS.md is an open, cross-vendor instruction-file format ('a README for agents') that has been adopted by over 60,000 open-source projects, making it the de facto standard rival/complement to CLAUDE.md-style project instruction files.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://agents.md/ (primary)
Quote: "a dedicated, predictable place to provide the context and instructions to help AI coding agents work on your project ... used by over 60k open-source projects"
Verifier evidence (high): The claim survives adversarial checks on all fronts. (1) Quote support: agents.md (fetched 2026-07-14) describes AGENTS.md verbatim as "A simple, open format for guiding coding agents" and a "README for agents," "used by over 60k open-source projects," matching the claim. (2) Cross-vendor status is confirmed, not just self-asserted: the format emerged from OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google Jules, Cursor, and Factory, is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, and is supported by 20+ agents including VS Code, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Devin, and Aider; OpenAI's own announcement (openai.com/index/agentic-ai-foundation/) independently repeats the 60,000+ adoption figure. (3) Independent verification of the headline number: I ran the GitHub code search the site links to (filename:AGENTS.md NOT is:fork NOT is:archived) via the GitHub API and got total_count=157,952 with incomplete_results=false — so "over 60k" is not marketing inflation; it is conservative/understated as of July 2026 (roughly 2.6x the claimed floor; note raw file-count can include multiple/nested AGENTS.md per repo, but even discounting heavily it clears 60k). (4) Not outdated: figure dates from the format's Aug 2025 launch and current counts exceed it. Minor caveat: "de facto standard rival/complement to CLAUDE.md" is an interpretive framing rather than a quoted fact, but it is reasonably supported by the multi-vendor adoption and Linux Foundation stewardship. The only self-interested element (the site is the format's own marketing page) was neutralized by primary-data verification.

### [8] AGENTS.md emerged from a collaboration including OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google's Jules, Cursor, and Factory, and is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation — i.e., governance of the format itself has been formalized into a neutral foundation.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://agents.md/ (primary)
Quote: "emerged from collaborative efforts across the AI software development ecosystem, including OpenAI Codex, Amp, Jules from Google, Cursor, and Factory ... now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation"
Verifier evidence (high): Claim survives adversarial check. (1) Quote support: agents.md itself states verbatim that AGENTS.md "emerged from collaborative efforts across the AI software development ecosystem, including OpenAI Codex, Amp, Jules from Google, Cursor, and Factory" and "is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation" — the claim is a faithful restatement, not an overreach. (2) Independent corroboration: the Linux Foundation's own press release (Dec 9, 2025, linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation) announces the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) anchored by contributions of Anthropic's MCP, Block's goose, and OpenAI's AGENTS.md; OpenAI (openai.com/index/agentic-ai-foundation/) and Anthropic (anthropic.com/news/donating-the-model-context-protocol-and-establishing-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation) published matching announcements; the MCP blog (2025-12-09) confirms the same structure. Platinum members include AWS, Anthropic, Block, Bloomberg, Cloudflare, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI. (3) No contradicting or qualifying sources found; the Dec 2025 event is current as of July 2026. One minor nuance: AGENTS.md was formally contributed by OpenAI (it is described as "OpenAI's AGENTS.md" in the LF release), so "collaboration" describes the format's ecosystem origins while the foundation donation itself was OpenAI's — this does not contradict the claim that governance is now formalized under a neutral foundation.

### [9] The spec prescribes hierarchical instruction resolution: nested AGENTS.md files in monorepos, with the nearest file in the directory tree taking precedence, and cites OpenAI's main repo containing 88 AGENTS.md files as a real-world example.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://agents.md/ (primary)
Quote: "Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence and every subproject can ship tailored instructions."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified directly against the primary source (https://agents.md/, fetched 2026-07-14). The spec site's FAQ states verbatim: "Place another AGENTS.md inside each package. Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence and every subproject can ship tailored instructions." and, in the same section, "For example, at time of writing the main OpenAI repo has 88 AGENTS.md files." Both components of the claim — (1) nested per-package AGENTS.md with nearest-file precedence for monorepos, and (2) the OpenAI main repo's 88 AGENTS.md files cited as a real-world example — are exact restatements of the spec's own text, not an overreach. The claim is appropriately hedged in that it attributes the 88-file figure to the spec ("cites"), matching the source's "at time of writing" framing rather than asserting the count as an independently verified current fact. Source quality is appropriate: agents.md is the canonical spec page maintained by OpenAI and partners, i.e., a primary source for what the spec prescribes. One minor caveat: "prescribes" is slightly strong — the nested-file guidance appears in the FAQ as recommended convention, and actual precedence behavior depends on each agent implementation (the spec itself notes agents read the nearest file, but AGENTS.md is a convention, not enforced). This nuance does not rise to refutation since the claim accurately reports what the spec says.

### [10] AGENTS.md ties instruction files to verification gating: agents are expected to execute programmatic checks listed in the file and fix failures before finishing a task.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://agents.md/ (primary)
Quote: "Yes—if you list them. The agent will attempt to execute relevant programmatic checks and fix failures before finishing the task."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified verbatim on the primary source: agents.md's FAQ answers "Will the agent run testing commands found in AGENTS.md automatically?" with exactly "Yes—if you list them. The agent will attempt to execute relevant programmatic checks and fix failures before finishing the task." (fetched 2026-07-14; the site is current, now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, originating from OpenAI/Amp/Google/Cursor/Factory). The claim's wording "agents are expected to execute... and fix failures before finishing" is a faithful paraphrase of the spec's own normative statement, and the "expected to" framing correctly avoids asserting guaranteed compliance — the FAQ itself says "attempt." One legitimate qualifier: the mechanism is advisory, not mechanically enforced gating — independent commentary (e.g. modelbehaviors.substack.com "AGENTS.md gets it wrong in 2 ways"; umesh-malik.com 138-repo study) documents that agents routinely skip or ignore such instructions, so "verification gating" should be read as the format's prescribed expectation, not deterministic enforcement. That caveat qualifies but does not contradict the claim as stated, since the claim describes what AGENTS.md prescribes ("agents are expected to"), which is exactly what the primary source says.

### [11] Anthropic's Agent SDK exposes lifecycle hooks (including PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit) as callback functions that can deterministically validate, log, block, or transform agent behavior at defined points in the agent loop.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview (primary)
Quote: "Run custom code at key points in the agent lifecycle. SDK hooks use callback functions to validate, log, block, or transform agent behavior. **Available hooks:** `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, and more."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched the cited primary source (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview) on 2026-07-14. The Hooks tab contains the supporting quote verbatim: "Run custom code at key points in the agent lifecycle. SDK hooks use callback functions to validate, log, block, or transform agent behavior. Available hooks: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, and more." All six hook names in the claim appear exactly. The page additionally demonstrates a working PostToolUse callback (HookMatcher(matcher="Edit|Write", hooks=[log_file_change]) in Python; hooks: { PostToolUse: [{ matcher: "Edit|Write", hooks: [logFileChange] }] } in TypeScript), confirming the callback-function mechanism. The only word not literally in the quote is "deterministically," which accurately paraphrases Anthropic's standard framing of hooks as user-defined code executed at fixed lifecycle points rather than prompt-level guidance; it does not overreach the source. Source is current first-party documentation for Anthropic's own product — appropriate quality for the claim's strength. No contradicting evidence exists; the claim is neither outdated nor promotional.

### [12] Anthropic treats CLAUDE.md (or .claude/CLAUDE.md) as the memory/instruction-file mechanism for project context, loaded via filesystem-based configuration from .claude/ in the working directory and ~/.claude/, with a settingSources/setting_sources option to restrict which sources load.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview (primary)
Quote: "The SDK also supports Claude Code's filesystem-based configuration. With default options the SDK loads these from `.claude/` in your working directory and `~/.claude/`. To restrict which sources load, set `setting_sources` (Python) or `settingSources` (TypeScript) in your options. ... Memory | Project context and instructions | `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`"
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview live on 2026-07-14. The page contains the supporting quote verbatim in its "Claude Code features" section: "The SDK also supports Claude Code's filesystem-based configuration. With default options the SDK loads these from `.claude/` in your working directory and `~/.claude/`. To restrict which sources load, set `setting_sources` (Python) or `settingSources` (TypeScript) in your options." The adjacent feature table lists "Memory | Project context and instructions | `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`", linked to /en/agent-sdk/modifying-system-prompts. The claim is a near-literal restatement of Anthropic's own current primary documentation — first-party source of the highest quality for a claim about Anthropic's own prescriptions. Only refutation angle found: earlier Agent SDK releases (v0.1.0, ~Sept 2025) required opting in via settingSources to load filesystem settings, but the current doc explicitly states defaults now load from both .claude/ and ~/.claude/, so the claim matches present behavior. No contradicting or qualifying credible source found; not a marketing statement.

### [13] The SDK supports multi-agent orchestration via subagents defined with specialized instructions and restricted tool lists, invoked through an Agent tool, with subagent messages carrying a parent_tool_use_id field for attribution to a specific subagent execution.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview (primary)
Quote: "Spawn specialized agents to handle focused subtasks. Your main agent delegates work, and subagents report back with results. ... Messages from within a subagent's context include a `parent_tool_use_id` field, letting you track which messages belong to which subagent execution."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview and https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents live on 2026-07-14. The supporting quote appears verbatim on the overview page. All claim components are confirmed by the primary source: (1) AgentDefinition requires a `prompt` ("The agent's system prompt defining its role and behavior") = specialized instructions; (2) the `tools` field restricts tool access ("Specify tools: agent can only use listed tools"), plus `disallowedTools`; (3) "Claude invokes subagents through the `Agent` tool, so include `Agent` in `allowedTools` to auto-approve subagent invocations" — invocation via an Agent tool; (4) "Messages from within a subagent's context include a `parent_tool_use_id` field" appears on both pages, with code examples checking `msg.parent_tool_use_id` for attribution to a subagent execution. Docs are current (reference Claude Code v2.1.198+ behaviors). Minor nuance only, not a refutation: the tool was renamed from "Task" to "Agent" in Claude Code v2.1.63 and some legacy fields (system:init tools list, permission_denials) still say "Task" — the claim's "Agent tool" phrasing matches current behavior. Official Anthropic SDK docs are the authoritative primary source for this API-surface claim; no contradicting evidence found.

### [14] Governance of tool access in the Agent SDK is enforced deterministically at the harness level via a permissions system: allowed_tools pre-approves tools, and agents can be configured to allow safe operations, block dangerous ones, or require approval for sensitive actions (e.g., a read-only agent limited to Read/Glob/Grep).
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview (primary)
Quote: "Control exactly which tools your agent can use. Allow safe operations, block dangerous ones, or require approval for sensitive actions. ... This example creates a read-only agent that can analyze but not modify code. `allowed_tools` pre-approves `Read`, `Glob`, and `Grep`."
Verifier evidence (high): Supporting quote verified verbatim on the live primary source (code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview, Permissions tab, fetched 2026-07-14): "Control exactly which tools your agent can use. Allow safe operations, block dangerous ones, or require approval for sensitive actions" and "`allowed_tools` pre-approves `Read`, `Glob`, and `Grep`" with the read-only agent code example. The claim's precise wording ("pre-approves") matches documented semantics: the harness evaluates deny rules -> allow rules -> permission mode deterministically before tool execution (confirmed on the dedicated permissions page, code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions). Adversarial check found closed GitHub issues (claude-agent-sdk-typescript#115 Dec 2025, claude-agent-sdk-python#361 Nov 2025) reporting allowed_tools failing to restrict Edit/Write/Bash — but both repros set permissionMode "bypassPermissions", which by documented design approves all tools; this qualifies rather than refutes the claim. Caveat for synthesis: "read-only agent limited to Read/Glob/Grep" holds only when the permission mode denies unlisted tools (SDK non-interactive default, disallowedTools, or dontAsk mode); allowed_tools alone is a pre-approval allowlist, not a hard restriction, and is inert under bypassPermissions.

### [15] The SDK provides persistent session state across exchanges — sessions can be resumed by session ID or forked to explore alternatives, with session state stored as JSONL on the local filesystem (versus an Anthropic-hosted event log for Managed Agents).
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview (primary)
Quote: "Maintain context across multiple exchanges. Claude remembers files read, analysis done, and conversation history. Resume sessions later, or fork them to explore different approaches. ... **Session state** | JSONL on your filesystem | Anthropic-hosted event log"
Verifier evidence (high): Live fetch of https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview (2026-07-14) confirms all elements verbatim: (a) Sessions capability text "Maintain context across multiple exchanges... Resume sessions later, or fork them to explore different approaches"; (b) working code example showing resume via captured session_id (ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=session_id) after reading session_id from the init SystemMessage); (c) the "Agent SDK vs Managed Agents" comparison table row "**Session state** | JSONL on your filesystem | Anthropic-hosted event log". The claim is a faithful, non-overreaching paraphrase of authoritative primary vendor documentation that is current as of today; no contradicting evidence exists, and the mechanism (session transcripts stored as JSONL under ~/.claude/projects, resumable/forkable) matches observable Claude Code behavior.

### [16] GitHub's Copilot desktop app isolates each parallel agent session in its own git worktree, making worktree isolation the concurrency-safety mechanism for multi-agent work.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/github-copilot-app-the-agent-native-desktop-experience/ (primary)
Quote: "Every session runs in its own git worktree, a real, isolated copy of your branch."
Verifier evidence (high): Primary source verified: GitHub's official blog post (June 2, 2026) states verbatim "Every session runs in its own git worktree, a real, isolated copy of your branch. This helps parallel agent sessions work without stepping on each other" and "The app handles every worktree for you: no manual setup, no cleanup, no branch juggling." Corroborated independently by InfoQ (infoq.com/news/2026/06/github-copilot-app/), the official github/app repository README, and the GitHub Desktop 3.6 changelog (June 26, 2026). Claim is current: the app reached general availability across all Copilot plan tiers on July 7, 2026. Only nuance: worktree isolation is the mechanism for LOCAL parallel sessions; cloud sessions use isolated GitHub-hosted environments instead — a qualification, not a contradiction, since the claim concerns desktop multi-agent concurrency.

### [17] GitHub's cloud coding agent defaults to deterministic permission-gating on every write action, with fully autonomous 'autopilot' mode as an explicit opt-in after trust is established.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/github-copilot-app-the-agent-native-desktop-experience/ (primary)
Quote: "By default, the cloud agent asks permission before each write action. Switch to autopilot once you have established trust."
Verifier evidence (high): Primary source verified by direct fetch: github.blog post "GitHub Copilot app: The agent-native desktop experience" (June 2, 2026) contains the exact quote "By default, the cloud agent asks permission before each write action. Switch to autopilot once you have established trust." Corroborated by official GitHub Docs pages ("Allowing GitHub Copilot CLI to work autonomously" autopilot concept page; "Responsible use of GitHub Copilot cloud agent") and by github/copilot-cli issue #1810 referencing the shipped "Enable autopilot mode dialog," proving autopilot is a real opt-in mode, not vaporware. No contradicting or qualifying sources found. Only caveat: "deterministic" is the claimant's gloss, not GitHub's word — but a mandatory per-write permission prompt is harness-enforced gating, so the gloss is accurate, not overreach. Claim is current (5 weeks old at review time) and non-extraordinary product-behavior description backed by primary source plus docs.

### [18] GitHub's 'Agent Merge' feature implements git-level enforcement of task completion conditions: the agent may drive CI back to green, address review feedback, and merge only when user-specified conditions are met.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/github-copilot-app-the-agent-native-desktop-experience/ (primary)
Quote: "Then Agent Merge helps carry that pull request through review, checks, and merge... You choose how far Copilot should go: drive CI back to green, address feedback, or merge when your conditions are met."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified by fetching the primary source directly: github.blog post "GitHub Copilot app: The agent-native desktop experience" (published June 2, 2026) exists and describes Agent Merge with matching language — it "helps carry that pull request through review, checks, and merge," monitors CI, tracks required reviewers, addresses failing checks, and users "choose how far Copilot should go: drive CI back to green, address feedback, or merge when your conditions are met." The claim is a faithful paraphrase, not an overreach. Independently corroborated by InfoQ (infoq.com/news/2026/06/github-copilot-app/), Help Net Security (June 8, 2026), and the github/app repository. Two qualifiers: (a) the Copilot app is in technical preview (Pro/Pro+/Business/Enterprise), not GA; (b) "git-level enforcement" is slightly interpretive — Agent Merge is agent automation gated on GitHub's existing merge conditions (required checks/reviewers) rather than a new enforcement primitive. Neither qualifier contradicts the claim's substance.

### [19] GitHub ships persistent cross-session, cross-surface agent memory as of mid-2026 via features named 'Memory++' and '/chronicle', spanning the desktop app, CLI, VS Code, and github.com.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/github-copilot-app-the-agent-native-desktop-experience/ (primary)
Quote: "Memory++ and `/chronicle` give Copilot continuity across devices and over time."
Verifier evidence (high): Independently fetched the raw HTML of the cited github.blog post (HTTP 200) and confirmed the exact sentence: "Memory++ and /chronicle give Copilot continuity across devices and over time. Query context from sessions started in the app, CLI, VS Code, or on GitHub." The post is genuine — the GitHub Copilot app was announced at Microsoft Build 2026 (June 2, 2026) and is corroborated by independent coverage (InfoQ 2026/06, Thurrott, DevOps.com). The claim's cross-surface scope (app, CLI, VS Code, github.com) restates the source verbatim rather than overreaching. Caveats that qualify but do not refute: (1) the Copilot app is in "technical preview," so "ships" means preview availability, not GA; (2) "Memory++"/"/chronicle" have little third-party documentation yet — GitHub docs describe the underlying "Copilot Memory" feature (repo-scoped, 28-day expiry, public preview Jan–Mar 2026), suggesting Memory++ is the newer extension announced at Build. Vendor blog is the appropriate primary source for a claim about what the vendor announced and named.

### [20] Unanimous multi-agent consensus is not evidence of correctness: 80+ agents (including ten dedicated adversarial reviewers) unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module, and only a single empirical test killed it — motivating a mandatory deterministic empirical validation gate rather than prompt-level consensus as the final arbiter.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049 (primary)
Quote: "ten dedicated reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL’s CMS module; it was killed only by a single empirical test, motivating the mandatory empirical gate."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified against the primary source PDF (arXiv:2604.19049, 'Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery', A. Agarwal, Apr 2026). All claim elements appear verbatim: (1) '80+ agents—including dedicated adversarial reviewers—unanimously endorsed a Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module that did not exist'; (2) 'Ten dedicated agents—including a senior-tier arbiter—unanimously confirmed a CMS Bleichenbacher padding oracle (CVSS 5.9)... One test killed what 80+ agents' reasoning could not'; (3) 'This failure drove the addition of mandatory empirical validation (Stage C)'; (4) the consensus-is-not-correctness framing is the paper's own: 'shared priors can manufacture apparent consensus.' The 80+ figure, absent from the supporting quote, is confirmed in the paper body (Sec 4.2 and discussion). Claim is current (Apr 2026) and not marketing. Caveat: single-author non-peer-reviewed preprint with self-reported case study, but the claim attributes it as such and does not exceed the source.

### [21] A Cross-Model Critic — an agent from a different model family given minimal context — catches correlated training-data errors that same-family review misses: in the libfuse campaign it found correctness errors in 3 of 19 (~16%) fixes that same-family review had approved, and surfaced 3 additional bugs same-family review missed.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049 (primary)
Quote: "In the libfuse campaign specifically, CMC found correctness errors in 3/19 (∼16%) same-family-approved proposed fixes and independently surfaced 3 bugs that same-family review had missed"
Verifier evidence (medium): Verified against the primary source. arXiv 2604.19049 ("Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery", Abhinav Agarwal) exists and contains the supporting quote verbatim: "CMC found correctness errors in 3/19 (~16%) same-family-approved proposed fixes and independently surfaced 3 bugs that same-family review had missed." The full text confirms these were proposed FIXES (not defect findings), matching the claim's framing, and names Codex (a different model family) as the cross-model critic: "Codex (a different model family) found 3 bugs that same-family review missed and identified correctness issues in 3 of 19 proposed fixes (16%)." The 'correlated training-data errors' mechanism is the paper's own stated rationale (same-family generative and review blind spots are correlated), so the claim does not overreach the source. The paper is current (April 2026) and corroborated in spirit by independent cross-model-review literature (e.g., ResearchGate "Cross-Model LLM Code Review: Should you use Claude to review Codex or vice versa?"; nhimg.org "Cross-model AI code review exposes the limits of single-model judgment"). No contradicting evidence found. Caveats that keep confidence below high: single-author arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed), one campaign, small n (19 fixes / 3 errors), no independent replication — but the claim is explicitly scoped to "the libfuse campaign," so source strength matches claim strength.

### [22] Zhipu AI explicitly frames GLM-5 as a paradigm shift from 'vibe coding' to 'agentic engineering', i.e., positioning the model for autonomous end-to-end software engineering rather than interactive assisted coding.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15763 (primary)
Quote: "We present GLM-5, a next-generation foundation model designed to transition the paradigm of vibe coding to agentic engineering."
Verifier evidence (high): Verified against the primary source (arXiv 2602.15763, fetched 2026-07-14). The paper's actual title is "GLM-5: from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering" (GLM-5 Team, Zhipu AI/Tsinghua, submitted 2026-02-17, v2 2026-02-24), and the abstract states verbatim: "We present GLM-5, a next-generation foundation model designed to transition the paradigm of vibe coding to agentic engineering." The claim's gloss (autonomous end-to-end SWE vs interactive assisted coding) is directly supported by the abstract's further statement that GLM-5 shows "unprecedented capability in real-world coding tasks, surpassing previous baselines in handling end-to-end software engineering challenges." Web search found no contradicting or qualifying sources; independent coverage (Hugging Face papers page, Webkul, Medium) corroborates the framing. The claim asserts only how Zhipu frames/positions the model — which the primary source proves — not that the model achieves full autonomy, so the marketing-language nature of the tagline does not refute it. Current as of July 2026 (GLM-5 released Feb 2026 as Zhipu's flagship).

### [23] GLM-5's agentic capability is trained via a new asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that decouples generation from training, plus novel asynchronous agent RL algorithms for long-horizon interactions — indicating Zhipu invests in model-side RL training for agency rather than harness-side scaffolding.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15763 (primary)
Quote: "we implement a new asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that drastically improves post-training efficiency by decoupling generation from training. Furthermore, we propose novel asynchronous agent RL algorithms that further improve RL quality, enabling the model to learn from complex, long-horizon interactions more effectively."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15763 directly: it is the GLM-5 technical report ("GLM-5: from Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering," GLM-5 Team, submitted 2026-02-17, v2 2026-02-24), and the supporting quote appears verbatim in the abstract — both "asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that drastically improves post-training efficiency by decoupling generation from training" (built on the slime framework / decoupled rollout engines from GLM-4.5) and "novel asynchronous agent RL algorithms... enabling the model to learn from complex, long-horizon interactions more effectively." The factual core is thus supported by the primary source, which is the correct source class for a claim about the lab's own training method, and the claim is current (Feb 2026 flagship report, ~5 months old as of July 2026). The interpretive clause ("rather than harness-side scaffolding") is a hedged inference ("indicating") not stated in the paper, but it is consistent with Zhipu's documented posture of shipping GLM coding models to run inside third-party harnesses (Claude Code-compatible coding plans) instead of a proprietary harness, and no contradicting evidence surfaced in search. Caveat: the efficiency/quality gains are self-reported by the GLM-5 team and not independently verified, but the claim asserts only the existence/use of the training approach, not superiority.


## Refuted claims (for transparency)
- "An adversarial, stage-gated multi-agent review pipeline (Refute-or-Promote) killed roughly 79% of ~171 defect candidates before disclosure over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets, with an 83% prospective kill rate on a consolidated-protocol subset (n=30), demonstrating that most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives that structured adversarial gating can filter out." (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049, vote 1-2)

## Instructions
1. Identify claims that say the same thing — merge them, combine their sources.
2. Group related claims into coherent findings. Each finding should directly address the research question.
3. Assign confidence per finding: high (multiple primary sources, unanimous votes), medium (secondary sources or split votes), low (single source or blog-quality).
4. Write a 3-5 sentence executive summary answering the research question.
5. Note caveats: what's uncertain, what sources were weak, what time-sensitivity applies.
6. List 2-4 open questions that emerged but weren't answered.

Structured output only.

content.text: All 24 confirmed claims are provided in the task; the work here is deduplication, grouping, and synthesis. Merging and grouping now.

input.summary: As of July 2026, coding-agent governance has converged on a clear architecture across Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub/Microsoft: short, hierarchical, nearest-file-wins instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, the latter now a Linux Foundation-stewarded cross-vendor standard used by 60k+ projects); an explicit split between advisory prompt-level instructions and deterministic harness-level enforcement (lifecycle hooks, permission gates, Stop-hook verification gates); runnable pass/fail checks as the primary quality mechanism with an escalation ladder from in-prompt iteration to hard gates; and git-worktree isolation as the standard concurrency-safety mechanism for parallel multi-agent work. Adversarial-review research (Refute-or-Promote, arXiv 2604.19049) supplies the strongest citable warning: 80+ agents unanimously endorsed a non-existent OpenSSL vulnerability that only an empirical test killed, so consensus and LLM review must be subordinate to deterministic empirical validation, ideally with a cross-model critic to break correlated blind spots. The one verified non-Western data point (Zhipu's GLM-5) shows a divergent bet on model-side asynchronous agent RL rather than harness-side scaffolding. For a 2026 governance-kit rewrite, the actionable prescriptions are: aggressively prune instruction files (Anthropic's removal test; OpenAI's 32 KiB hard cap), split guidance into nested per-directory files, move every must-happen rule from prose into hooks/permission gates, gate task completion on executable checks rather than agent self-report or reviewer consensus, and isolate parallel agents in worktrees with fresh-context, diff-only adversarial reviewers whose findings are treated as noisy signals, not mandates.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus: instruction files must be short, and vendors now enforce or prescribe brevity. Anthropic officially instructs users to aggressively prune CLAUDE.md — the test for each line is 'would removing this cause mistakes?' — warning that bloated files cause the model to ignore instructions. OpenAI enforces the same principle deterministically: Codex caps combined AGENTS.md content at 32 KiB by default (project_doc_max_bytes) and silently stops loading files beyond it, with docs recommending splitting instructions across nested directories rather than growing one file.
findings.evidence: Anthropic (verbatim): 'Keep it concise. For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!' OpenAI (verbatim): 'Codex stops adding files once the combined size reaches the limit' (32 KiB default); silent truncation corroborated by openai/codex issue #7138. Both are live primary vendor docs fetched 2026-07-14.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus: hierarchical, nearest-file-wins instruction resolution is the standard structure. Codex resolves instructions via global scope (~/.codex, AGENTS.override.md then AGENTS.md) followed by a walk from Git root to cwd, at most one file per directory, nested files overriding ancestors. The AGENTS.md spec prescribes the same for monorepos — nested per-package files with nearest-file precedence — citing OpenAI's main repo containing 88 AGENTS.md files as a real-world example.
findings.evidence: Codex docs verbatim: 'Files closer to your current directory override earlier guidance' and 'Codex includes at most one file per directory.' agents.md verbatim: 'Agents automatically read the nearest file in the directory tree, so the closest one takes precedence' and 'at time of writing the main OpenAI repo has 88 AGENTS.md files.'

findings.claim: AGENTS.md has become the de facto cross-vendor instruction-file standard with formalized neutral governance: it emerged from OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google's Jules, Cursor, and Factory, is used by over 60,000 open-source projects (verifier's independent GitHub search found ~158k matching files, so the figure is conservative), and is now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation (announced Dec 2025 alongside Anthropic's MCP donation). Codex treats it as the primary governance mechanism, automatically reading AGENTS.md files before doing any work — though loading is mandatory while compliance remains prompt-level and advisory.
findings.evidence: agents.md verbatim: 'used by over 60k open-source projects'; 'now stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation.' Codex docs verbatim: 'Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work.' Verifier independently ran GitHub code search (total_count=157,952, incomplete_results=false) and cross-checked LF press release of 2025-12-09. Note: the mandatory-read claim carried a 2-1 vote; open Codex issues (#6502, #6666, #4466) document inconsistent application despite reading.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement: every major Western vendor draws an explicit line between advisory prompt instructions and deterministic harness enforcement, and prescribes moving must-happen rules to the harness. Anthropic states CLAUDE.md is advisory while hooks are deterministic ('use hooks for actions that must happen every time'); a Stop hook can block turn completion until a check passes (overridden after 8 consecutive blocks). The Agent SDK exposes lifecycle hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit) as callbacks that validate, log, block, or transform behavior, plus a deterministic permissions system (allowed_tools pre-approval, e.g. a read-only agent limited to Read/Glob/Grep). GitHub's cloud agent defaults to permission-gating every write action, with autonomous 'autopilot' as explicit opt-in after trust is established.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.' GitHub verbatim: 'By default, the cloud agent asks permission before each write action. Switch to autopilot once you have established trust.' SDK docs confirm hook names and permissions semantics verbatim. Caveat: allowed_tools is a pre-approval allowlist, not a hard restriction — it is inert under bypassPermissions mode.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on verification gating: the top prescription across vendors is a runnable pass/fail check as the arbiter of completion, with an escalation ladder of strictness. Anthropic's lead best practice is giving the agent a verifiable check (tests, build exit code, linter, screenshot diff) and choosing how hard it gates: in-prompt iteration → /goal conditions re-checked every turn → deterministic Stop hooks → second-opinion verification subagents. The AGENTS.md spec ties instruction files to the same expectation: agents execute programmatic checks listed in the file and fix failures before finishing. GitHub's Agent Merge extends gating to the git level: the agent drives CI back to green, addresses review feedback, and merges only when user-specified conditions are met.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes.' agents.md FAQ verbatim: 'The agent will attempt to execute relevant programmatic checks and fix failures before finishing the task.' GitHub verbatim: 'drive CI back to green, address feedback, or merge when your conditions are met.' Caveats: AGENTS.md check-running is prescribed expectation, not mechanical enforcement; Agent Merge rides GitHub's existing merge conditions rather than adding a new enforcement primitive, and the Copilot app is in technical preview.

findings.claim: Convergent consensus on multi-agent orchestration: git-worktree isolation is the industry-standard concurrency-safety mechanism, and orchestrator/subagent patterns are first-class. Anthropic recommends worktree-isolated parallel sessions, agent teams with a team lead, and Writer/Reviewer session pairs; its Agent SDK supports subagents with specialized instructions and restricted tool lists, invoked via an Agent tool, with parent_tool_use_id attribution per subagent execution. GitHub's Copilot desktop app independently converged on the same design: every parallel agent session runs in its own git worktree, managed automatically.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'Worktrees: run separate CLI sessions in isolated git checkouts so edits don't collide.' GitHub verbatim: 'Every session runs in its own git worktree, a real, isolated copy of your branch.' SDK docs confirm AgentDefinition (prompt + tools restriction) and parent_tool_use_id verbatim. GitHub app reached GA across Copilot tiers 2026-07-07; cloud sessions use hosted isolated environments instead of local worktrees.

findings.claim: Adversarial review works but has sharply documented limits, yielding three citable design rules. (1) Reviewer over-reporting: Anthropic warns that a reviewer prompted to find gaps will report some even when the work is sound, and chasing every finding causes over-engineering; its prescribed mitigation is a fresh-context subagent that sees only the diff and criteria. (2) Consensus is not correctness: in the Refute-or-Promote study, 80+ agents including ten dedicated adversarial reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module; only a single empirical test killed it — motivating a mandatory deterministic empirical-validation gate rather than prompt-level consensus as final arbiter. (3) Cross-model critique breaks correlated blind spots: a critic from a different model family found correctness errors in 3 of 19 (~16%) fixes that same-family review had approved, plus 3 additional missed bugs, in the libfuse campaign.
findings.evidence: Anthropic verbatim: 'A reviewer running in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and the criteria you give it... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering.' Paper verbatim: 'ten dedicated reviewers unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module; it was killed only by a single empirical test' and 'CMC found correctness errors in 3/19 (~16%) same-family-approved proposed fixes.' Confidence capped at medium because arXiv 2604.19049 is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint with small n and no replication (the cross-model claim drew only medium verifier confidence), and the same paper's headline ~79%-kill-rate claim was refuted in verification. The Anthropic over-reporting warning alone is high-confidence.

findings.claim: Memory persistence is converging on layered mechanisms: instruction-file memory plus resumable session state, with cross-surface memory as the 2026 frontier. Anthropic treats CLAUDE.md/.claude/CLAUDE.md as the project memory/instruction mechanism, loaded via filesystem configuration (.claude/ and ~/.claude/, restrictable via settingSources); its SDK persists session state as local JSONL, resumable by session ID or forkable to explore alternatives (versus an Anthropic-hosted event log for Managed Agents). GitHub ships persistent cross-session, cross-surface agent memory ('Memory++' and '/chronicle') spanning desktop app, CLI, VS Code, and github.com as of mid-2026.
findings.evidence: SDK docs verbatim: 'Resume sessions later, or fork them to explore different approaches' and 'Session state | JSONL on your filesystem | Anthropic-hosted event log.' GitHub verbatim: 'Memory++ and /chronicle give Copilot continuity across devices and over time. Query context from sessions started in the app, CLI, VS Code, or on GitHub.' Caveat: Memory++//chronicle have little third-party documentation and ship in technical preview; underlying Copilot Memory was repo-scoped with 28-day expiry in its Jan-Mar 2026 public preview.

findings.claim: Verified Western-vs-Chinese divergence (limited to one data point): Zhipu AI positions GLM-5 as a paradigm shift 'from vibe coding to agentic engineering' — autonomous end-to-end software engineering — and invests in model-side capability via a new asynchronous RL infrastructure that decouples generation from training plus novel asynchronous agent-RL algorithms for long-horizon interactions. This contrasts with the Western pattern of harness-side governance (hooks, gates, permissions); Zhipu ships GLM coding models to run inside third-party harnesses (including Claude Code-compatible plans) rather than building its own enforcement layer.
findings.evidence: GLM-5 technical report abstract (GLM-5 Team, Zhipu AI/Tsinghua, Feb 2026) verbatim: 'designed to transition the paradigm of vibe coding to agentic engineering' and 'we implement a new asynchronous reinforcement learning infrastructure that drastically improves post-training efficiency by decoupling generation from training.' The model-vs-harness contrast is a hedged inference consistent with Zhipu's shipping posture, not a stated claim; training gains are self-reported. This is the only Chinese-lab claim that survived verification — Moonshot, DeepSeek, Tencent, MiniMax, and Qwen practices remain unverified, so the divergence generalization rests on n=1.

input.caveats: Coverage is uneven: verified claims exist only for Anthropic, OpenAI/AGENTS.md, GitHub/Microsoft (Copilot), one independent arXiv methodology paper, and Zhipu AI. Nothing survived 3-vote verification for Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), Microsoft AutoGen, NVIDIA NeMo/agent toolkits, xAI, Moonshot AI, DeepSeek, Tencent Hunyuan, MiniMax, Alibaba Qwen, Nous Research, Fundamental Research Labs, tinygrad/George Hotz, or the open harnesses (OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin) — so the 'convergent consensus' findings reflect the verified subset, not the full requested survey, and the Western-vs-Chinese divergence rests on a single lab (Zhipu). The 'Ornith-1.0 LLM' named in the question could not be verified to exist and no claims about it were produced; it should be treated as unverifiable rather than real. arXiv 2604.19049 (Refute-or-Promote) is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint with self-reported case studies; its headline claim (~79% kill rate over a 31-day campaign) was refuted in verification (1-2 vote), so only its OpenSSL false-consensus anecdote and cross-model-critic result should be cited, with the small-n qualifier. Several GitHub features (Copilot app cloud agent, Agent Merge, Memory++//chronicle) are in technical preview, and Memory++//chronicle lack third-party documentation. AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md compliance is prompt-level everywhere: mandatory loading does not mean enforced obedience (documented Codex issues show inconsistent application; the 32 KiB truncation is silent). All vendor-doc claims were verified live on 2026-07-14 against fast-moving documentation; specifics (8-block Stop-hook override, 32 KiB default, hook names) may change within months.
openQuestions: What do Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), the major Chinese labs beyond Zhipu (Moonshot Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek, Tencent Hunyuan, MiniMax, Qwen), and leading open harnesses (OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin) actually prescribe for instruction files, hooks, and verification gating — and does the model-side-RL vs harness-side-scaffolding divergence hold beyond the single verified Zhipu data point?

How well do agents actually comply with instruction-file directives in practice — given documented Codex issues of reading-but-ignoring AGENTS.md and Anthropic's admission that long files get ignored, is there rigorous empirical data on compliance rates versus file length, structure, or placement?

Does the Refute-or-Promote result (unanimous multi-agent consensus on a non-existent vulnerability; cross-model critics catching ~16% bad fixes) replicate at scale in peer-reviewed or industrial settings, and what is the optimal cost/precision trade-off for mandatory empirical-validation gates in a drop-in governance kit?

How will AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md conventions reconcile under the Agentic AI Foundation's stewardship — will a unified resolution/precedence spec emerge (including standardized hook or check-declaration syntax), and should a 2026 governance kit target AGENTS.md as primary with CLAUDE.md as an alias?
